M3 Magnetic Circuits (Chapter 3, first half)

Why this matters in the exam: Q2 of every final is “Magnetic Circuits and Transformers” (20 marks), and Q2a is always the magnetics part: Jun23 Q2a was 9 marks (C-core reluctance and , air-gap energy, iron-loss scaling) and Jun24 Q2a was 7 marks (gapped toroid and , maximum voltage from the back-emf equation, slot force). The mid-semester assessments weight it even more heavily. The 2023 quiz Q3 and Q4 were 10/40 marks and the 2024 test Q4 and Q5 were 12/40. The back-emf equation also sets up the transformer parts (Q2b, Q2c): turns, , , and how open-circuit quantities scale with . So the full 20 marks of Q2 lean on this pack.

1.3 Where the energy sits (lecture 3.3.6–3.3.7)

is the same in the iron and in the gap. The energy density is , so the iron stores as much per m³ as air. The lecture C-core (two 0.5 mm gaps, 0.5 m of iron with ) stores 0.895 J in the gaps and 0.0895 J in the iron. That is ten times more in 1 mm of air than in 500 mm of iron. Ratio check: . The energy splits in the same ratio as the reluctances (and as the mmf drops).

1.4 DC current versus AC voltage (lecture 3.4.4)

  • DC current drives the coil. is fixed. depends on the gap. A bigger gap gives less flux and less force.
  • AC voltage drives the coil. is fixed by the back-emf equation. The current becomes whatever is needed: with . A bigger gap gives the same flux but more current.

This is why Practice Q3.8(f) gives the same 6.974 V with and without the gap.

1.5 Saturation and the B–H curve (lecture 3.5)

  • Iron is linear () up to about 1.6–2 T. Above the knee collapses towards 1.
  • and (since ). So the B–H curve is also the – curve.
  • When AC voltage drives the coil, the flux stays sinusoidal (it is the integral of ). Above rated voltage, or below rated frequency, enters the knee. The magnetising current then becomes large and peaky (distorted), which overheats the copper. This is the voltage rating of a coil or transformer.
  • Saturation also breaks every “” rule: , constant, and so on. Comment on it whenever a computed is above about 1.6 T.

1.6 Iron loss and how it scales (lecture 3.6)

  • Hysteresis: . This is the energy to reverse the domains each cycle. You reduce it with better material and heat treatment.
  • Eddy current: . Induced currents circulate in the conducting core. You reduce it with thin insulated laminations (, so halving the thickness cuts it by 4) and with silicon steel (higher resistivity). Eddy loss dominates at high frequency.
  • Air has no iron loss because it is not conductive.

Raise B_max into the knee to see the loop flatten into saturation, then change f and compare how the hysteresis bar (∝ B²f) and the eddy bar (∝ B²f²) grow.

Scaling when V or f changes. Use from the back-emf equation.

Change

, same (i.e. , constant V/f) same
, same (unchanged)
both and given given

At fixed , both losses go as . That is why the core loss is modelled as a resistor with (Practice Q3.26b, Jun24 Q2c(iii): halve , so ).

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Miscounting gaps. Two C-cores separated by paper of 0.07 mm give mm and force area (2024 test Q4). A saw-cut slot in a toroid is one gap and one area (Jun24 Q2a(iii)). Two poles “with a 4 mm airgap between them” is one 4 mm gap (2023 quiz Q4).
  • rms versus peak in the back-emf equation. is rms and is peak. Do not multiply by , and do not put an rms flux density into it.
  • Putting reluctance into the back-emf equation. Gaps and change the current, not the voltage for a given . Jun24 Q2a(ii) needs only , , and .
  • Scaling total iron loss with one law. You must split into hysteresis and eddy first. Jun23 Q2a(iii) gives 30%/70% for exactly this reason. Scaling 12 W by a single factor loses all 3 marks.
  • Forgetting that changes with at fixed . “Same transformer, 60 Hz supply, same voltage” means drops by 5/6.
  • Area and length units. 20 cm² = m², not . For a toroid use . Diameter 2.5 cm means cm.
  • Rounding turns the wrong way. Round up when is a limit. Round the secondary turns to the nearest integer (, e.g. 33.8 becomes 34 in the 2024 test Q5c).
  • Not flagging saturation. If your answer implies –2 T, say that the linear model (, constant ) no longer holds.

2023 quiz Q7 (4 marks). Short-Answer Questions. Answer the following question using words only (that is, without using sketches or equations).

In designing a transformer using a given magnetic core, what is the process for selecting the number of turns on the primary winding for a given primary voltage? Carefully explain the results of using too few turns. How about if too many turns are used?

Solution
  • Process. The back-emf equation links the primary voltage, frequency, turns and peak core flux. For a given core area and supply, choose the number of primary turns so that the peak flux density sits just below the saturation level of the core material.
  • Too few turns. The peak flux density must be higher. The core saturates and the magnetising current becomes very large and distorted. The winding overheats.
  • Too many turns. The core runs at a low flux density, so it is under-used. The longer wire has more resistance, which raises copper loss and lowers efficiency, and can also cause overheating.

(Exam instruction: words only, so no equations or sketches.)

PQ 3.14 (practice questions). Answer the following questions about magnetics.

  1. Consider a magnetic core with an airgap. Where is the majority of energy stored?
  2. Iron losses are caused by changing magnetic fields in a conductive magnetic material. Are there any iron losses when air is exposed to a changing magnetic field?
  3. What are the two types of iron loss?
  4. Which type of iron loss is more important when magnetic cores are operated using high frequency currents and why?
  5. Why do motors and transformers normally use iron in the form of thin, insulated iron sheets rather than a solid core?
  6. What happens to the input current of an inductor as the AC voltage is increased such that the core goes into saturation?
Solution

  1. In the airgap (it has most of the reluctance, so most of the mmf and energy).

  2. No, because air is not conductive (no eddy currents) and has no magnetic domains (no hysteresis).

  3. Eddy-current loss and hysteresis loss.

  4. Eddy-current loss, because it is proportional to frequency squared, so it dominates at high frequencies.

  5. To reduce eddy-current losses: the insulated laminations break up the eddy-current paths.

  6. It increases rapidly and becomes distorted (peaky), because collapses and much more current is needed for each extra bit of flux.

These match the official answers.

MAGNETIC CIRCUITS (Ch3 first half)          mu0 = 4*pi*1e-7 H/m
mmf = NI = Phi * R_total = sum(H*l)          H = B/(mu_r mu0),  Phi = B*A
R = l/(mu_r mu0 A)   gap: mu_r = 1           series add; parallel Ra*Rb/(Ra+Rb)
L = N^2 / R_total     lambda = N*Phi = L*I    "infinite mu"  =>  R_total = R_gap
GAPS: saw cut / 2 poles "g apart" = ONE gap, area A once
      2 C-cores / U-core + armature = TWO gaps: l_g = 2g, force area = 2A
Energy  E = B^2/(2 mu0) * A * l_g (gap)  ; total = 0.5 L I^2 ; iron term has /mu_r
Force   F = B^2/(2 mu0) * A_force         ; hold mass: B = sqrt(2 mu0 m g / A_force)
Back-emf  E_rms = 4.44 N f B_pk A   (NO reluctance in it; B_pk ∝ V/(N f))
   N = V/(4.44 f B_max A) -> round UP; actual B = V/(4.44 N f A)
   V_max = 4.44 N f B_max A ;  new supply: N ∝ V/f ; N2 = N1*V2/V1 (nearest)
DC current fixes mmf (gap changes flux); AC voltage fixes flux (gap changes current)
Saturation ~1.6-2 T: current large and peaky, F∝I^2 and constant L fail
IRON LOSS  P_H ∝ B^2 f (hysteresis),  P_E ∝ B^2 f^2 (eddy; laminate, Si-steel)
   1) split known loss into H and E   2) new B (given, or B ∝ V/f)
   3) P_H2 = P_H1 (B2/B1)^2 (f2/f1),  P_E2 = P_E1 (B2/B1)^2 (f2/f1)^2   4) add
   Fixed f: P ∝ V^2 (hence R_C = V^2/P_FE).  Fixed V, f up: P_H ∝ 1/f, P_E constant
